Initially scheduled for full closure amid low Danube water levels and hence limited cooling water resources on July 31, the plant still keeps one of its two 680 MW reactors online. However, as the situation remains critical, Romania seeks emergency imports from Ukraine and prepares for measures to restrict national consumption. The experts expect low water levels to put at risk Cernavoda NPP’s operations at least until mid-August. The government of Romania on July 31 declared a nationwide state of alert in the energy system for the entire month of August, following the drop in electricity production caused by severe drought and the very low water levels of the Danube and rivers. Acting prime minister Ilie Bolojan warned that there is a risk of the second reactor of the Cernavoda NPP shutting down, which would mean the loss of approximately 20% of national energy production, Digi24 reported. PM Bolojan, who holds the interim portfolio of energy, also announced that Romania has discussed possible imports of electricity with Ukraine, where a surplus of power would be available. He stated that he discussed the situation on Friday with the deputy prime minister of Ukraine and minister of energy, Denis Shmîgal. “Today I discussed with the deputy prime minister of Ukraine, who also holds the energy portfolio, Mr Shmîgal, to support us in the coming period with production from one of Ukraine’s nuclear power plants. In this regard, Transelectrica and Nuclearelectrica will hold discussions for emergency aid from Ukraine during the evening hours,” PM Bolojan said………………. Special operations on the Danube are aimed at keeping Cernavoda NPP online as long as possible. Romania’s Naval Forces attempted on Sunday, August 2, to detonate a rock on the right bank of the Danube, in order to divert the water flow towards the Cernavoda NPP. Two explosions occurred, but they failed to break the rock. The military will resume the operation on August 3, with a larger load of explosives, the Ministry of Defense announced. “At this moment, the Ministry of National Defense is intervening with over 100 soldiers and 16 technical means to divert the course of the Danube towards the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant. EOD combat divers have successfully carried out the first tests, during which they detonated small explosive charges in a controlled manner,” the Ministry of National Defense announced in a statement on its Facebook page. According to Antena 3 , the authorities say that such a measure is needed because the extremely large rock blocks the course of the Danube, which can reach the Cernavodă power plant. The next step is the obstruction of another arm of the Danube (Bala Arm), with the aim of diverting part of its flow towards the arm passing by Cernavodă NPP (Old Danube). Thus, four barges loaded with approximately 500 tons of stone will be controlledly sunk on the Bala Arm, which will allow a larger volume of water to be directed to the Old Danube from the Bala Arm. Separately, dredging works will be carried out on the channel delivering water to Cernavoda NPP. iulian@romania-insider.com https://www.romania-insider.com/romania-divert-danube-nuclear-plant-august-2026 Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook August 6, 2026 - Posted by Christina Macpherson | climate change , EUROPE No comments yet. Photograph: Historic England Heathrow third runway Heathrow expansion ‘is threat to England’s largest surviving medieval barn’ Exclusive: campaigners warn 600-year-old New Barn at Harmondsworth could be ‘shaken to pieces’ by vibrations Dalya Alberge Sat 22 Aug 2026 20.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 22 Aug 2026 20.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Six hundred years after it was built, England’s largest surviving medieval timber-framed barn could now be “shaken to pieces” by aircraft vibrations, campaigners warn. The public has until 1 September to submit objections to the Heathrow airport expansion, which could threaten the survival of the New Barn at Harmondsworth, considered a remarkable example of medieval architecture. The barn was built in 1426 and was bought in 2011 by English Heritage, which is staging a major conference in September. Its significance lies in its extraordinary scale, as well as the near-complete survival of its medieval structural timbers. It is nearly 60 metres long, 12 metres wide and 11 metres tall, with 13 massive oak trusses holding up the roof. It was described as a “cathedral” by the former poet laureate Sir John Betjeman, who was struck by the size and atmosphere of this magnificent structure. One of the conference speakers is Justine Bayley, English Heritage’s former archaeological scientist. She told the Guardian that the boundary of the extended airport is barely a few hundred metres from the barn, which “could be shaken to pieces by the vibrations from airplanes taking off”. The barn was built to store agricultural produce exactly 600 years ago this year. The land had been bought in 1391 by the then bishop of Winchester. Bayley said: “It’s not plus or minus 10 years or half a century. How many late medieval buildings do we know when they were built? Its structural timbers are more than 95% original. Most of the big medieval barns and other large timber-framed buildings have been repaired, and you’re lucky if 50% of the original timbers are there.” View image in fullscreen Former poet laureate Sir John Betjeman described the barn as a ‘cathedral’. Photograph: Historic England If the Heathrow expansion goes ahead with a third runway, she questions whether the barn is “still going to be here”. The government is consulting on amendments to the Heathrow expansion national policy statement, for which it is now seeking comments. It is an ongoing process which includes Heathrow airport running its own consultation later this year. Bayley, who chairs the Stop Heathrow Expansion campaign, said: “The Department for Transport (DfT) has declared that Heathrow is a critical national infrastructure and therefore all the legislation to do with environmental limits and climate change and so on can be just ridden roughshod over because they’ve decided that it was more important that Heathrow’s expansion goes ahead. “It bulldozes two villages and makes another two or three uninhabitable. It’s all there in the detail that’s been consulted on. This is effectively the government setting out the hoops to jump through. They’re moving the goalposts.” Noting that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously expressed concerns over the Heathrow expansion – because the plans divert infrastructure investment “away from the north and traps it in London” – she said that opposing the plans will be “difficult but not impossible”. She argued that actual measurements of the vibrations from the current north runway have not been taken, although it is a similar distance from the nearby village of Longford, which would be demolished: “Longford has dreadful vibrations. You can stand in a house and feel it coming up through the floors and through your feet. Heathrow was saying ‘no, you’re imagining things, that’s not true’. Just because they don’t want it to be true. If they were to actually monitor vibrations and the noise, that would throw up warnings for the barn.” Christian Hughes, who understands that his Longford home will be demolished if the third runway goes ahead, fears for the barn’s survival as a relatively new house in a nearby hamlet has developed “significant cracking” from the vibrations of passing aircraft. He said: “We can actually feel planes departing before we can hear them. The low frequency is so bad. My house is 200 years old. Longford has houses that date back to the 1600s and even older. They’ll be demolished as well. It’s criminal.” View image in fullscreen The barn’s structural timbers are more than 95% original. Photograph: Historic England Marian Campbell, art historian and former curator at the Victoria and Albert museum said: “This visually stunning medieval building, the New Barn, is improbably located close to Heathrow’s runways. It is an exceptionally rare survival. Apart from its enormous size … it is exceptional too because documents tell us exactly when it was built – 1426 – where the trees came from and who paid for it.” A Heathrow spokesperson said: “We will continue to listen to and work with our local communities as we progress our expansion plans, including the opportunity to take part in our own public consultation later this year. While the Great Barn is outside the new airport boundary, the DCO process will look in detail at a wide range of potential impacts and any necessary mitigations, to ensure this crucial project is delivered responsibly.” English Heritage and the Friends of the Great Barn at Harmondsworth are hosting the conference in the barn and the adjacent church of St Mary on 5 September. It will include papers on the barn’s construction and recent archaeological investigations. A DfT spokesperson said: “Views on the potential impacts of expansion – including on the environment, heritage sites and neighbouring communities – will be carefully considered as part of our consultation before any final decisions are taken.” Explore more on these topics Heathrow third runway England Heathrow airport Air transport Airline industry English Heritage news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution
